title: Every nation kneeling
hookLine: you'll see every nation kneeling, called to its record (45:28)

lines: ALL OF THEM, ON THEIR KNEES.
cards: Every crowd that ever lived, from every century and language, all at once, on their knees. Not standing to cheer. Not lying flat.

Kneeling, the way a person kneels while waiting to hear something that matters: a verdict, a name, a result that can't be changed anymore. Surah Al-Jathiyah takes its name from that one picture, and it isn't a quiet one.
Al-jathiyah means the kneeling one, and today's verse is where the picture comes from.

teach.b: Verse twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "And thou wilt see each nation crouching, each nation summoned to its record." Pickthall says crouching; the Arabic, jathiyah, describes sitting on the knees.
Commentators explain it as the posture of fear and suspense: waiting, unable to stand and unwilling to lie down. Notice the grammar. It isn't humanity as one blur.
It's each nation, umma by umma, each summoned to its own record, its kitab. The next verse says the record speaks against them with truth, because what they did was being written down.
So the book here isn't a scripture handed down. It's a ledger written up, the record a people made with their own hands.
Some commentators also connect it to the individual record every person receives, which other verses describe as given in the right hand or the left. One more detail.
In the Muslim prayer there's a moment of sitting back on the knees, between the prostrations and at the end.

teach.h: THE SAME KNEELING IN EVERY PRAYER.
teach.b: So a posture this surah attaches to the Last Day is one Muslims take in every prayer. Some readers draw that line directly: the person who kneels willingly now is practicing for the kneeling that won't be optional.
The surah doesn't say it like that, and it's fair to mark the difference. But the shape of the body is the same.
And the question the verse leaves is a calm one: what is my page saying, while there's still time to write on it?

how: In every Muslim prayer, worshippers sit back on their knees between the two prostrations and for the final testimony; some also use the quiet of that posture to ask forgiveness.

o: kneeling, waiting on the knees for what comes
lying face down, forehead on the ground
bowing low, hands on the knees in prayer

s: the book in 45:28 is a scripture sent down
commentators read it as the record of deeds, written up, not handed down.
the verse speaks of each nation separately
each umma is summoned to its own record.

games.q: you are in the scene of 45:28, one among every nation. what posture does the verse give you?
games.why: jathiyah: kneeling in suspense, each nation summoned to its own record.

practice: If your knees allow, kneel on the floor, sitting back on your heels; if not, sit in a chair with your hands on your knees, and feel the weight settle.

Without judging, look back over the last week as if it were a page: one line you're glad is written there, and one you'd like to write differently. If you pray, you can ask forgiveness for the second.

wordCard.voice: Jathiyah: the posture of waiting on the knees, each people summoned to the record it wrote, in 45:28. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: kneeling; the word that names surah 45.

carryVoice: Your line: each called to its book. Each nation, its own record, written by its own hands. See you tomorrow.
